messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Soldier
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Marisol had been thirty-nine when she came to treatment, a married Latina soldier who had spent much of her adult life in disciplined routines and structured environments, and she was unsettled by how little control she still felt over her own body and attention after the storm. The disaster had struck years earlier while she was on duty, when an ordinary weather system turned violent and then, in her telling, became something unrecognizable: wind hammering so hard against the building that the walls seemed to shudder, rain coming in sheets, and then the sharp, punishing crack of loud noises she could not initially identify amid the chaos. Police arrived during the aftermath to secure the area and direct people where to go, and Marisol remembered the sight of uniforms moving through flooding, debris, and darkness as one of the images that stayed fixed in her mind. What she had once assumed would be a manageable emergency became a prolonged scene of uncertainty, with no clear way to leave and nowhere that felt safe enough to stand still. In the months that followed, she noticed that certain weather conditions now carried the force of that night back into the present. A humid, heavy sky or the same dense gray light before a storm could make her stomach tighten before she had even named why. She found herself bracing when thunder rolled in the distance or when a door slammed too hard, and loud noises at work or on the street made her jump in a way that embarrassed her because, as she put it, they were “the kind of sounds that shouldn’t matter.” Police presence was especially difficult; seeing officers at a checkpoint, near her base, or outside a public building could pull her attention away from whatever she was doing and leave her feeling as if she were back in the confused, secured perimeter of the disaster site.

Over time, Marisol began arranging her life around the possibility of another sudden emergency. Before entering a restaurant, church, waiting room, or even a new section of the base, she would automatically identify exits and decide where she could move if something happened. She did this before she felt comfortable anywhere, and she knew she did it without thinking, as if her body would not allow her to settle until she had mapped the nearest way out. Even in familiar places she kept doing it, scanning corners, doorways, and the people around her for signs of danger. She described herself as always watching, always listening, and always catching herself on alert for the next loud sound that might make her flinch. At work, this meant she was never fully at ease during briefings, drills, or crowded movements through shared spaces, because her attention would split between the task at hand and the exits, alarms, or unusual noises around her. Friends and family noticed that she seemed tense in places where she used to relax, and she had begun choosing seats near doors and avoiding situations where she could not quickly orient herself. The practical habits gave her a temporary sense of readiness, but they also made ordinary outings feel effortful and left her exhausted by the end of the day.

Marisol spoke about herself with a harshness that had become part of her private language. Since the event, she had come to believe that her reactions showed she was a lousy coper, someone who should have adapted by now instead of still feeling unsettled by weather, noise, and police. She was pained by how unlike herself she felt when she was startled by a sound that others barely noticed, and she sometimes interpreted her own vigilance as proof that something essential in her had become damaged. At moments she felt like an object rather than a person, as though she were moving through her days on autopilot, reacting to whatever happened around her without any real say in it. What frightened her most was the conviction that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. The storm had shown her, in a way she had never expected, how quickly conditions could change and how little her own effort could guarantee safety. That sense followed her into daily life, so that even calm days carried a quiet expectation that something could go wrong without warning.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was not only tired of being on guard but increasingly distressed by how much of her life had become organized around reminders of the disaster. She wanted to be able to sit through a stormy afternoon without bracing, to hear a sudden noise without jolting, and to see police without feeling pulled back into that flooded, chaotic scene. She came to treatment hoping to feel more like a person again than a body waiting for impact, and she was most afraid that if nothing changed she would keep living as though the storm were still coming.
